prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single nucleobases in DNA without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: I keep base editing as a single-part prize for Liu. After round 1 the chemical argument is stronger, not weaker: Somfai, Zou, Brzezinski and Linke all accept that the novelty lies in enzyme design, namely a nucleobase deaminase tethered to a catalytically impaired Cas protein and an adenine deaminase evolved by directed evolution to act on DNA, which no natural enzyme does. That is reactivity control on a single nucleobase, and it differs mechanistically from the double-strand cleavage rewarded in 2020. It has been reproduced by many independent groups in about ten years and has reached patients. Five of eight members include it, always with Liu alone, which tells me the attribution is the least disputed part of a contested case. The chair asks whether a second part is wanted. I do not think so: the proposed pairings (C-N coupling, electron tunnelling, nanopores) share no scientific thread with base editing and would read as a trade, which several colleagues themselves concede. A single achievement can be explained to a broad audience in one sentence.
statement.case_against: The 2020 CRISPR prize remains the strongest counterweight, and the targeting machinery of base editors is still CRISPR, as Chabes rightly says. The clinical record is short and off-target and bystander editing are still being measured. Attribution is the other weakness: Komor and Gaudelli were first authors of the decisive papers, and Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID was an independent parallel invention. Naming Liu alone is a defensible convention of crediting the leader of the programme, but it is a judgment, and I accept that the committee could reasonably prefer a different cut.

responses.point: Chabes rejects a Liu-only prize as clean, argues the targeting machinery is still CRISPR, and ranks degraders above base editing because their mechanism is better defined, while noting no PROTAC is approved.
responses.response: The point about the targeting machinery is fair, and it is why the citation must be worded around nucleobase chemistry and not genome editing in general. But the chemistry that is new, the deaminase on DNA and the evolved TadA, is exactly what the 2020 prize did not cover. On attribution I still read Target-AID as a citation caveat. Your own response to Somfai accepts that a clean attribution is a real virtue, and B058 has one name on which five members agree, while B008 asks us to choose three from eight, including the Crews and Deshaies versus Ciulli question you raise yourself. I agree degraders are a game-changer in waiting, and that is why B008 stays my first alternative; with no approved degrader and the PROTAC and glue strands still unresolved, I would not put it ahead of base editing this year.

responses.point: Zou moved to Liu alone, pushes back that Komor and Gaudelli were first authors and not merely trainees, and wants the dates and overlap with Kondo and Nishida examined.
responses.response: I accept the correction on Komor and Gaudelli: they were first authors of the decisive papers, and I should not have called them merely trainees. My argument for Liu alone is the committee's convention of crediting the principal investigator who conceived and directed the programme, and the three-person cap, not a claim about their contribution. On Kondo and Nishida, the dates matter and the expert reports should check them, but I would still treat Target-AID as an independent cytidine deaminase-nickase result that was narrower in scope, whereas the adenine base editor, which made A-to-G conversion possible at all, came only from the Liu programme. That is the difference I would want stated.

responses.point: Somfai now treats B058 as the better second part of a shared prize with Pd-catalysed C-N coupling, and argues the novelty must be answered with the deaminase engineering and not the clinical story.
responses.response: I agree that the deaminase engineering is the answer to the 2020 question, and I have rebuilt my case on it. Where I differ is the pairing. B030 is mature, clean at two names and arguably overdue, and I would support it on its own. But Linke and Chabes both ask what is new in kind beyond the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and a flask-to-genome pairing that joins two unrelated achievements invites exactly the trade you warn about. I would rather see each stand alone than see B058 used to carry B030. If the committee wants a two-part prize, I would want it argued that each part would win a prize by itself, and I do not think B030 has yet been shown to be distinct in kind from 2010.

responses.point: Linke, as Chair, proposes pairing Liu with Bayley and Akeson on nanopores as two engineered molecular tools for DNA, one that writes and one that reads, and asks that the citation stress nucleobase chemistry.
responses.response: I agree on the citation wording and have kept it on nucleobase conversion. On the pairing, I find the writes and reads symmetry attractive as rhetoric but the chemistry content of the nanopore part is, as you say yourself, less decisive than the instrumentation and enzyme-motor engineering. The attribution problem you describe (Deamer, Branton and Kasianowicz outside the cut, and the question of whether Branton is still living) is unresolved, and I would not want to fix names before it is checked. Taking a weak attribution into a two-part prize would cost the whole configuration more than a single clean part gains.

responses.point: Sparr moved to B064 first and asks how I would handle the Kondo and Nishida claim in a citation, saying a Liu-only prize is possible but more exposed than B064.
responses.response: My answer is that the citation names the principle and not the people: the programmable chemical conversion of nucleobases in DNA without double-strand cleavage. The background text can then acknowledge Target-AID as an independent contemporaneous realisation, which is normal for parallel inventions. On exposure, I think B064 is at least as exposed: you say yourself that DLin-MC3-DMA and later lipids tie to MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and that a Vancouver trio may look like a patent-priority judgment. B058 faces one contested attribution question, B064 faces three and the 2023 overlap. I still value the pKa-tuned lipid design principle and would not oppose it later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts Liu alone, or insists on Komor and Gaudelli, or Kondo and Nishida; I have not seen the exact dates and what each group had demonstrated at the time.
How much weight the 2020 CRISPR prize carries against a technique whose targeting still relies on Cas proteins.
Whether the clinical record will have lengthened enough to show durability and acceptable off-target outcomes.
Whether a two-part prize, which several colleagues prefer, would be defensible if each part is judged on its own.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B058. My ties to Warshel and to the Uppsala RNA and ribosome community do not touch base editing. I note a bias toward computational methods that applies to B014, which I list only as an alternative, and I have no tie to any candidate named in B058, B008 or the other shortlisted parts.
